definition: Multi-objective Optimization minimizes several objectives at once, such as validation error, runtime, memory, and model size. Because objectives can conflict, the result is usually a Pareto set of non-dominated trade-offs rather than one universally best configuration.
intuition: There may be no single winner: a model can be more accurate but slower, smaller but less accurate, so keep only trade-offs that another candidate does not dominate.
mathematical_foundation:
$$
\min_{\lambda \in \Lambda} c(\lambda) = (c_1(\lambda), \ldots, c_m(\lambda)), \qquad m \ge 2
$$

A configuration is Pareto-dominated when another is no worse on every objective and strictly better on at least one.
advantages: Makes resource and quality trade-offs visible instead of hiding them in one score.
Returns alternatives suited to different deployment constraints.
limitations: Scaling and weighting objectives can change the apparent trade-off.
There may be many non-dominated solutions and no single default choice.
